ECE 6390 / Navigation

CDMA near–far effect

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows why a weak code can remain obscured by a much stronger code despite small cross-correlation.

A correlator matches the desired code and ideally reduces other codes by their cross-correlation. If the unwanted signal has voltage amplitude Ai and normalized cross-correlation magnitude |ρ|, its residual amplitude is Ai|ρ|.

Power is amplitude squared, so the output signal-to-interference ratio is Ps/(Pi|ρ|²). A tenfold interfering voltage means a hundredfold interfering power. Use 20 log₁₀ for amplitude ratios and 10 log₁₀ for power ratios.

Power control can reduce near–far imbalance in communication networks. Navigation receivers also need sufficient front-end dynamic range and interference resistance. A desired digital correlation cannot recover information lost through analog saturation.

Example

An interferer 20 dB stronger in power has ten times the desired voltage amplitude. With |ρ| = 0.1, its residual voltage equals the desired voltage, giving 0 dB output SIR in this one-interferer model.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. For an interferer 40 dB stronger in power and |ρ| = 0.01, what is the residual power relative to the desired signal?

    Multiply 10⁴ by (0.01)².

    The residual powers are equal, so output SIR is 0 dB.

    2. Why do many interferers require more than inspecting a single cross-correlation number?

    Each signal brings its own power, delay and code phase.

    Their leakage contributions depend on received powers, cross-correlations, relative phases, timing and data transitions. Multiple-access interference and noise must be combined in the appropriate statistical model.
